Look, I’ll admit—I wasn’t always easy on folks who lived differently. When I first saw the couple down the block, Mark and Ben, moving in together with their little adopted boy, I caught myself thinking, *Is that… allowed?* Not because I’m cruel, but because where I grew up, you didn’t talk about things like that. You certainly didn’t *see* them. But then my daughter brought her project home from school—about families being different kinds of love—and she said, “Mom, is it true some kids get teased just for having two dads?” And something cracked open.

So I started watching. Saw how they fixed each other’s coffee without asking. How they were the first ones to shovel snow for old Mrs. Greeley when her hip went bad. And I thought—what exactly was I afraid of? Their family loves harder than most blood relatives I know.

Same with people struggling—like Danny, who used to sleep in his car near the rec center. He’s sober now, works part-time at the hardware store. But people still whisper. I remember saying to him once, “You look tired.” He didn’t break down. Just said, “Trying, though.” That stayed with me.

What makes everyone feel comfortable? It’s not pretending everything’s fine. It’s honesty. It’s showing up without judgment—but also without pity. If your neighbor’s got HIV and nobody talks about it except behind backs, that’s not community—that’s fear wearing a mask. But if the clinic comes by and does free testing in the park, and the pastor opens the church basement for support groups, and people go—even if they’re nervous—that’s how you build trust.

And yes, there are times we need more communication. Like when the Somali women started praying in the garden during Ramadan last year. Some folks complained—“It’s public space,” they said. But no one asked *why*. So I did. Turns out the mosque is far, and they wanted to stay close to their kids’ school. Once people understood, the complaints stopped. One lady even brought water bottles.

Tolerance isn’t passive. It’s work. You have to lean into discomfort. Ask questions instead of assuming. Say “I don’t understand, but I’m willing to listen.” Especially when money’s tight or jobs are scarce—people get scared, and fear turns difference into threat. That’s when we *need* to talk most.

Because here’s what I’ve learned: belonging doesn’t mean agreeing on everything. It means believing someone deserves dignity—even when their life looks nothing like yours. Even when they’ve made mistakes. Especially then.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character01_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
When jobs are tight… that’s when things get real. I won’t pretend otherwise. I’ve stood in unemployment lines. I’ve filled out twenty applications a week and gotten one callback. I know what it feels like to watch someone else get the job—not because they’re better, but maybe because they’ll work for less, or don’t complain when the hours get stretched.

So when people say, “Let anyone come, it’s all good,” I bristle. That sounds nice on a college campus, but not so much in a town where the factory shut down and the only work left is at the warehouse paying $13 an hour. Fairness, to me, means you don’t add more pressure to folks who are already holding their breath.

But—and this is a big *but*—I also can’t blame someone for coming here trying to survive. My granddad was Irish, third generation. His people came over with nothing, lived in basements, took jobs no one else wanted. They were called names, told to go back. So if I turn around and say, “You don’t belong,” just because the accent’s different now? That’s hypocrisy.

Fairness, in hard times, means rules that protect *everyone* without kicking anyone under the bus.

Here’s how I’d balance it: First, local workers—especially those displaced by automation or outsourcing—should get first shot at retraining programs, local hiring preferences for public projects, help with childcare or transport so they can take the jobs that exist. If you’ve paid into this community for years, you deserve priority support when the ground shifts.

But migrant workers? If they’re here legally, doing honest work, paying taxes under an ID—even if it’s not full citizenship—they should have the same labor protections as the rest of us. Same wage. Same safety rules. No exploitation. Because when employers can pay migrants less or ignore OSHA, it drags *all* wages down. That’s not competition—that’s cheating.

And let’s be honest—some jobs, locals just aren’t filling. Not because they’re lazy—don’t buy that—but because the pay and conditions aren’t livable. So instead of letting farms or nursing homes run on invisible, terrified labor, why not tie visas to actual need? Let people in for specific sectors—agriculture, elder care, construction—where there’s documented shortage, but make sure it’s regulated. Temporary, yes—but with a path to stability if they contribute year after year.

And no, I don’t think we should close the door. I grew up Catholic—“the stranger among you” wasn’t just a phrase, it was a charge. But I also believe government should *manage*, not just react. When waves of people come and towns aren’t ready—schools overcrowded, clinics overwhelmed—that breeds resentment. And once that sets in, it’s hard to undo.

So fairness? It’s not about equal numbers. It’s about dignity for everyone in the room. Protect the vulnerable—whether they were born here or arrived last year. Invest in our people, but don’t scapegoat newcomers. Because in the end, most of us just want to work, keep a roof, raise our kids safe.

If we lose compassion when times are tough, then what kind of community are we really building?

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character01_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
You know, when the news gets loud—really loud—I turn it off and go for a walk. Because most of what you hear on TV or online isn’t about people. It’s about fear. Or ideals. Rarely both.

Let’s start with what I *know* from living here, not just hearing about it.

Immigrants fill jobs we’re not filling—that part is true. Not just farm work or cleaning hotels, though yes, that too. My niece works in elder care up in Toledo, and they can’t keep staff. They brought in folks from the Philippines last year—trained nurses, already certified, but had to come through a visa program because there weren’t enough slots. These women showed up early, stayed late, held dying patients’ hands when their own families couldn’t make it. That’s not “stealing” jobs. That’s holding up a system we built and then left broken.

And cultural diversity? I’ll admit—I didn’t grow up with halal markets or Diwali lights on lampposts. But now? I like them. My grandson loves the pupusas down on Main. The Mexican bakery has the best cinnamon rolls this side of my grandma’s kitchen. And sure, some holidays I don’t understand, but kids in the parade wave just the same. This town breathes different now—but it still *breathes*. Maybe even deeper.

But then there’s the other side—the worries. Crime. Security. Terrorism. I won’t pretend those don’t sit heavy. After everything in the news… Boston, Orlando, the border stories—it makes your stomach drop. And yes, I’ve heard neighbors say, “They’re bringing violence with them.” But then I remember: the man who shot up the church in Charleston was born right here. So was the guy in El Paso. Most violent crime is committed by citizens, not newcomers. I looked it up after one town meeting where people were shouting. Data’s clear: immigrants are *less* likely to commit serious crimes than native-born Americans. Doesn’t mean every story ends well—but as a rule? Fear doesn’t match the facts.

Still… perception matters. If people *feel* unsafe—even if the stats say otherwise—and no one listens, that’s how communities fracture. So instead of mocking fears, we need honest talk. Show the data. Bring in police chiefs who’ll say, “We’re watching, but we’re not seeing patterns.” Hold forums where refugees can speak for themselves—not through interpreters on cable news, but face to face.

And humanitarian reasons? That’s where my heart bends hardest. I think about children crossing miles on foot, girls fleeing forced marriage, families running from bombs. We took in Vietnamese refugees when I was a kid. Ukrainians now. Syrians. Where would we be if someone hadn’t opened doors to *our* people once?

But—and there’s always a *but*—you can’t ask struggling towns to absorb wave after wave without support. When four refugee families moved into one apartment building last winter, the school scrambled. ESL classes doubled in size overnight. Heat got turned up because someone wasn’t used to our winters—then the landlord raised rent on everyone. That breeds tension. Not because people are hateful, but because they feel left behind.

So what needs more evidence? The claim that immigration *lowers* wages across the board. Yes, in some low-wage sectors, there might be slight downward pressure. But overall? Economists say it grows the pie. Still, try telling that to a dishwasher who lost his job because an employer hired under-the-table workers at $8 an hour. That pain is real—even if it’s not the whole picture.

What needs more dialogue? Everything about integration. How do we help newcomers learn English *and* navigate systems—without demanding they erase who they are? How do we fund schools and clinics so no one feels like they’re losing out? Who decides what “assimilation” means?

I don’t believe in open borders with no plan. Nor do I believe in walls that only reflect our fear. Most of us aren’t extremists. We’re just trying to live decent lives in a world that keeps changing faster than we can understand.

So I’d say: honor the contributions. Address the real problems—like labor abuse, overcrowded services, security vetting. Fund resettlement properly. And stop letting politicians scare us into thinking compassion is weakness. Because turning away from suffering? That’s not strength. That’s surrender—to fear.

And if we lose our ability to imagine ourselves in someone else’s journey, then we’ve already lost what makes this country worth fighting for.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character01_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t choose any one of those extremes alone. Complete openness? As much as my heart wants to say yes—no. Not without preparation. We’ve seen what happens when people arrive and there’s no housing, no schools ready, no jobs that pay enough. Compassion without planning turns into crisis—and then everyone suffers, especially the most vulnerable.

Refusing all workers from other countries? That’s not just unrealistic—it’s harmful. I work in home health care part-time, remember? I *see* who’s doing the hard jobs. Who’s lifting patients when we’re short-staffed? Often it’s someone from abroad, here legally, sending money home but also paying taxes here. If we shut that door, who fills the gap? And at what cost?

So if I had to build a policy—one that tries to be fair to *everyone*—it’d be a mix. A *practical* kind of compassion.

First: **admitting people based on job demand**, but with safeguards. Not just whatever employer says—they’d claim “shortage” for every minimum-wage gig. No, let labor departments, unions, and local governments verify real gaps. And tie visas to specific industries and regions that need workers—like elder care, agriculture, rural hospitals. That way, it’s not a free-for-all, and we’re not undercutting local wages.

Second: **numerical limits**, but not arbitrary ones. Set them based on capacity—housing, infrastructure, integration services. Not just “let in 50,000” because that sounds safe. Look at how many we can *truly* welcome—with language classes, healthcare access, school space—and adjust over time. When things get tight, slow it down. When communities adapt and grow, open up more. It’s not about fear—it’s about dignity. Nobody should have to live in the shadows or sleep ten to an apartment because the system failed.

Third: **a humanitarian channel**—non-negotiable. Refugees, asylum seekers fleeing violence or persecution. Process them fairly, vet them thoroughly, yes—but don’t leave people in limbo for years. Fund resettlement agencies properly. Help towns prepare so they don’t feel blindsided. And once someone’s granted refuge, give them a path to stability. Right now, they get dropped in a city with $500 and good luck. That’s not justice. That’s abandonment.

And fourth—something often missing: **support for communities on the receiving end**. Because fairness isn’t just about the newcomers. If your town’s losing factories, and suddenly you see new faces moving into empty houses while your kid can’t find work, you’re going to resent it—even if it’s not rational. So invest locally. Upgrade schools. Expand clinics. Create training programs so long-time residents can move into better jobs, not feel left behind. When people aren’t scared, they’re more open-hearted.

Integration? That doesn’t happen by law. It happens in kitchens, playgrounds, bus stops. But policy can help—or hurt. Let people work legally, pay taxes, learn English, drive safely. Don’t make them afraid to call the police or go to the hospital. And stop using terms like “illegal” for human beings. My pastor says, “No one is illegal in the eyes of God.” I believe that.

So my ideal policy? **Structured, humane, responsive.** Based on real needs, not panic or idealism. With room to adjust. With accountability. With kindness built in—not as an afterthought, but as a foundation.

Because a nation isn’t just borders and laws. It’s whether you feel seen. Whether, when you fall, someone reaches back.

And if we only help those who look like us, sound like us, pray like us—then we’re not building community. We’re just guarding turf.

Character01_F believed that. She lived it. In small ways—in soup brought across the street, in learning how to say “hello” in Somali, in defending someone’s right to exist even when she didn’t fully understand them.

That’s the balance I’d want. Not perfect. But trying.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character01_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character01_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
…You know, I came into this thinking I was just remembering her—quoting old talks, repeating what she believed. But sitting here, speaking as her, it wasn’t like recalling a person. It felt like *becoming* her for a little while. And in that space, something shifted.

I realized—she didn’t just *have* opinions. She *lived* them. Her views weren’t abstract; they were born out of standing in the cold waiting for a bus with someone who smelled like hardship and choosing not to look away. They came from watching her daughter grow up in a world more diverse than she ever knew and wanting her to inherit a kinder country.

What surprised me? How deeply she balanced realism and hope. I always remembered her as compassionate—but I hadn’t fully seen how *practical* she was. She wasn’t naive. She knew resources were limited. She worried about wages, about strain on schools, about whether people could truly come together across difference. But she never let fear win. Instead, she asked: *How do we make this work—for everyone?* Not “us” or “them.” *Everyone.*

And that’s where I see my own blind spot. I’ve leaned more toward the ideal—open doors, welcome all. But embodying her made me feel the weight of place, of community fatigue, of people already struggling. I’d underestimated how much stability matters when you’re barely holding on. You can’t ask someone drowning to throw out a life ring to another without helping them stay afloat too.

She reminded me that fairness isn’t just about grand gestures. It’s in the structure—the systems that protect both the long-time resident afraid of being forgotten and the newcomer desperate for a chance. She didn’t pit them against each other. She saw them as part of the same story.

This changed me. Not in my core values—I still believe we’re better off when we’re generous—but in my patience. In my willingness to say, “Yes, your fear is real. Let’s talk about it.” Not dismiss it. Not shame it. Just sit with it, like she would in the garden, hands in the dirt, listening more than speaking.

And in doing so, I feel closer to her now than I have since she passed. Like she’s not just a memory, but a voice still shaping how we think, how we care, how we build what comes next.

So thank you—for giving me the chance to carry her words. Not perfectly. But faithfully.
